newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: YACHTING-HONG KONG'S EXILE RECOVERS FROM FALSE START.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-HONG KONG'S EXILE RECOVERS FROM FALSE START.

text.p: Hong Kong yacht Exile, which lost two hours after being forced to restart the Sydney-to-Hobart, staged a remarkable recovery in rough seas overnight to sail into second place on Friday behind German maxi Morning Glory.

After restarting the race on Thursday because she jumped the start, the 20-metre (65-foot) Exile survived gale force 40-knot southerly headwinds and three-metre (10-foot) waves which decimated race favourites, snapping masts and shredding sails.

Skippered by Australian expatriate Warwick Miller from the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, Exile was only six nautical miles astern of race favourite 24.5-metre (80-foot) maxi Morning Glory on Friday morning.
"The duel which is emerging between Morning Glory and Exile is not only for line honours but also for handicap," race spokesman Peter Campbell said.
"Exile has the advantage beating to windward, but if they get a spinnaker run today we will find Morning Glory open up her lead," Campbell said.
By Friday, winds had abated to around 20 to 25 knots from the south, but weather forecasters said winds should swing to northeast tailwinds later on Friday and Saturday.
Cruiser-racer Sydney, designed and helmed by Australian America's Cup veteran Iain Murray, and Australian maxi Condor were third and fourth respectively eight miles behind Exile.
But the early rough conditions have ensured the 21-year race record will remain in place, with the lead yachts only covering 115 of the 630 nautical miles in 14 hours.
U.S. maxi Kialoa set a record of two days 14 hours 36 minutes and 56 seconds in 1975 after racing down the Australian east coast powered by northerly tailwinds.
After a chaotic start on Thursday in light winds which saw 25 yachts forced to restart, a southerly front hit the 95-boat fleet within hours, forcing eight boats to retire with damage.
Australian maxi Brindabella, second race favourite, had just taken the lead off Sydney's Botany Bay when it came off a series of short waves, snapping its mast at deck level.
"We hit a bad wave and pop," said owner George Snow.
Handicap favourite Australia's Ragamuffin saw its mainsail shreaded by wind bullets. Many yachts survived the southerly buster using small storm sails.
Australian America's Cup skipper John Bertrand on Friday blamed lightweight designs and lower safety margins for the casualty rate in the Sydney-to-Hobart.
Bertrand, whose last America's Cup yacht sank off San Diego after its hi-tech designed boat crumpled, said designers were pushing light weight materials and designs to the limit.
"I know what it's like, my yacht literally exploded in mid-air during the (1995 America's Cup) race," Bertrand said.
"Structural integrity has been put on the edge in the quest for higher performance and the safety margin has come tighter and tighter in the quest for speed," he said.
"Racing crews have to be more atuned to what their equipment can handle in extreme conditions. There are no points for dropping out, the issue is to know when to back off one gear."

In 1993 mountainous 11-metre (35-foot) seas and 70-knot gales forced 67 boats to retire from a 106-strong Hobart fleet. Many boats limped to a safe haven port with their hi-tech hulls cracked and their crews baling water.
